title: Follow up qa-v1-theory-9c9e6db0baee9a4709ec3405
behavioral_concerns: follow up: Directory entries are masked to 0o700 during copy, but regular-file entries are written with their original Mode().Perm() bits intact, so a source file with group- or world-writable permissions such as 0666 or 0777 survives verbatim into the isolated workspace and weakens the 0700 containment promised by the parent directory.

evidence.summary: Directory branch masks permission bits to 0o700; file branch passes source Mode().Perm() unchanged to os.WriteFile.
evidence.output_digest: isolation.go:346 os.Mkdir(destination, info.Mode().Perm()&0o700) vs isolation.go:357 os.WriteFile(destination, data, info.Mode().Perm())

evidence.summary: Existing test asserts the copied file retains the source's 0o644 mode, locking in preservation rather than tightening.
evidence.output_digest: isolation_test.go:38-40 if copiedInfo.Mode().Perm() != 0o644 { t.Fatalf("copied mode = %v", copiedInfo.Mode().Perm()) }

evidence.summary: Parent and workspace root directories are created with 0o700, contrasting with files whose mode is preserved verbatim.

theories.claim: The bounded-tree copy preserves each source regular file's permission bits verbatim while masking directory permissions to 0o700, so a source file with group- or world-writable bits (e.g. 0o666 or 0o777) is reproduced in the isolated workspace with those bits intact, weakening the 0o700 containment advertised by the parent directory and isolated workspace root.
theories.basis: isolation.go:346 creates intermediate directories with `os.Mkdir(destination, info.Mode().Perm()&0o700)`, applying a 0o700 mask, but isolation.go:357 calls `os.WriteFile(destination, data, info.Mode().Perm())` for regular files without any masking. isolation.go:105 creates the parent with0o700, and isolation.go:108 uses `os.MkdirTemp(parent, ...)`, so the workspace root is0o700, but children may have wider bits. The test isolation_test.go:38-40 explicitly asserts `copiedInfo.Mode().Perm() != 0o644`, locking in preservation of source bits for the file case rather than tightening them.
theories.verification_surface: isolation.go:344-359 (file copy branch vs. directory branch); isolation_test.go:38-40 (test asserts preservation, not masking); isolation.go:105,108 (parent and root are 0o700)
theories.confirmation_condition: Read isolation.go:357 verbatim and observe no permission mask applied to the WriteFile call, paired with isolation_test.go:38-40 asserting that a 0o644 source becomes a 0o644 destination; directory branch at isolation.go:346 explicitly masks with &0o700, demonstrating the asymmetry.
theories.refutation_condition: isolation.go:357 applies an explicit mask such as &0o600 (or otherwise narrows perm bits) and isolation_test.go:38-40 is updated to match the narrowed bits; or a separate post-write chmod narrows bits for regular files.
theories.inconclusive_condition: Static reading is the only inspection surface available to a read-only investigator, so the mode bits that survive for arbitrary0o666/0o777 sources cannot be exercised dynamically here; only the literal code path and the existing assertion can be cited.
theories.safe_evidence_strategy: Quote the WriteFile mode argument and the Mkdir mask side-by-side and cite the test assertion that pins0o644 as the expected copied mode.

theories.outcome_reason: isolation.go:357 passes `info.Mode().Perm()` directly to `os.WriteFile` with no mask, while the sibling directory branch at isolation.go:346 explicitly masks with `&0o700`. isolation_test.go:38-40 asserts the copied file retains0o644, demonstrating that preservation (not narrowing) is the intended and locked-in behavior. The asymmetry between directory and file branches confirms that group/world-writable source bits survive into the workspace.
